lines.text: Imagine typing one sentence, like: build me a team that answers questions about my company. And getting back a working team of AI agents.
That is real today. But nobody answers the next question. Is it a good team?
Could a smaller team do better? Could it be cheaper?
This video explains a project that answers exactly that: neuro-san-esp. No background needed. We start from zero.
First, what is an AI agent? Think of a new employee on their first day.
They have a brain. Here, that is a large language model, like GPT, Claude or Gemini.
They have instructions, like a job description.
And they have tools, like a search box for the company's files.
Give them a question. They think, use their tools, and reply.
One employee can only do so much, so we build teams. Picture a restaurant kitchen.
The head chef takes the order and passes parts of it to specialists: one on the grill, one on sauces, one on desserts.
In AI, the head chef is called the front man, or coordinator. The cooks are specialist agents.
neuro-san, an open-source framework from Cognizant AI Lab, lets you describe a team in a simple config file, and it runs the whole team for you.
It even has a designer agent that writes the team for you, from one sentence.
Here is the gap. neuro-san's designer builds one team, and stops. It never measures it.
Nothing in the framework scores one team against another.
So you cannot say whether a 9-agent team beats a 5-agent team for the same job, or which AI model each agent should use.
It is like hiring a whole department without ever giving anyone a test.
This project supplies the missing half. It measures a team. Then it searches for a better one.

scenes.title: An exam no model has seen

lines.text: To measure a team, you need an exam.
But ask about a real company, and the model might answer from memory. Then you learn nothing about the team.
So the project invents a company: Meridian Logistics.
It has 24 depots, 40 contracts and 60 incidents, written up in 124 documents.
None of it exists anywhere else, so no model saw it in training. An open-book exam, on a book nobody has read.
A real question: “Incident INC-4413 affected a contract serviced by a depot. Who is that depot's manager?”
One document says the incident hit contract C-2113.
Another says C-2113 is serviced by depot D04, in Ashford.
A third says D04 is managed by R. Delacroix.
Four hops across three documents, like a detective following clues from one file to the next.
And because the company was generated by code, every answer is known to be correct.
Each team sits the exam, and three things are recorded.
Accuracy: how many answers are right.
Tokens: how many words the models read and wrote, which is what you pay for.
And size: how many agents are in the team.
These combine into one score, called fitness. Think of a report card: your marks, minus a small fine for being expensive, minus a tiny fine for being big.
One more fairness rule. If a team runs out of time, that is marked unfinished, not wrong. A student whose pen ran out did not give a wrong answer.
Now the search. The project borrows an idea from nature: evolution.
Each team's recipe is its genome: neuro-san's own config file, plus the model each agent uses. Every candidate is a real, runnable team.
To make new candidates, there are seven mutations.
Add an agent. Remove an agent. Rewire who talks to whom. Split one agent into two. Merge two into one. Switch searching on or off. And give an agent a different model.
It is like a chef changing one ingredient at a time, and tasting the result.
Some mutations make nonsense. An agent nobody can reach. A loop where agents call each other forever. Or no front man at all.
A validity gate throws those away. It never patches them.
Like a building inspector rejecting a house with no door.
So every candidate that reaches a real test is a team neuro-san would actually serve.
There is a catch. Every real exam costs money and time, because every answer calls a real AI model.
So it borrows ESP, Evolutionary Surrogate-assisted Prescription, from Cognizant AI Lab: built for problems where each real test is expensive.
Phase A: measure a few starting teams for real.
Phase B: train a Predictor that guesses a team's results from its shape.
Phase C: breed thousands of candidates and rank them with the Predictor. Free: zero AI calls.
Phase D: pay to test only the most promising few, and feed the results back into B.
It is like a car maker testing designs in a computer simulation, and only building the best ones for the real wind tunnel.
The Predictor is careful about what it learns. There is one small model per outcome. One guesses accuracy. One guesses token cost.
They read 13 features of a team's shape: how many agents, how deep, how many can search.
Fitness is then worked out with plain arithmetic. It is never learned. And the agent count is not predicted at all, because you can simply count it.
To choose parents, it uses a Pareto front. Think of buying a phone. One is cheapest, one has the best camera, one has the longest battery.
Any phone that no other phone beats on every count stays on the shortlist. Those teams get to breed.
Splitting the Predictor this way exposed a real problem.
The accuracy model ranks teams well, clearly better than chance. But the token model ranks them backwards. It calls the cheap teams expensive.
A single combined score had hidden that, because accuracy carried the average.
The fix is a gate. Each round, every prediction is compared with what shuffled, meaningless data would score. A predictor that loses to chance is muted for that round.
Like a weather forecaster who does worse than a coin flip on wind. You still listen for rain. You stop asking about wind.

scenes.title: Never grade on the questions you chose with

lines.text: The next trap is subtle. If you choose a winner with some questions, then report its score on those same questions, you fool yourself.
It is like a student who memorised last year's paper.
So the questions come from two separate halves of the company. 60 select questions choose. Judge questions only grade, never choose.
This rule changed the story. The first search, on 17 questions, found a champion scoring 94%.
On fresh questions it only tied the designer's team, at 2.2× the cost. Its gain came from a stronger model on the coordinator, not a better structure.
The project says so openly, and searched again.
So what did the improved search find?
On 100 judge questions, asked twice: a team of just two agents, a coordinator and one researcher, with a stronger model only on the researcher that reads the documents.
It scored 94.5%. The four-agent team neuro-san's designer would build scored 84.0%.
The small team used 37% fewer tokens.
On 17 questions it was right more often than the designer; on only 2, less often. Chance of that by luck: p = 0.0007.
Now the fine print, because good science shows it.
The stronger model costs more per token, so the winner cost 71% more per question, even with fewer tokens.
The designer's team was not tested with upgraded specialists. So we cannot yet say how much of the gain is structure, and how much is the model.
The search tool now returns 10 documents instead of 3, so these numbers are never compared with older runs.
The winner, 2cc4, is one hand-written starting team with its Arithmetic agent removed: one mutation, chosen by measurement. The Predictor was not used in the paid runs.
So the takeaway, on this benchmark so far: a small team, with the strong model where the hard reading happens, beat a bigger team of cheap specialists.

scenes.title: Dollars, a pool, and a $0 rehearsal

lines.text: The newest parts push this further.
Fitness can now be counted in dollars, from the provider's own bills. So a pricey model is charged what it really costs.
A per-question Predictor guesses a team's chance on each kind of question, and an ensemble shows how sure it is.
A pool benchmark is built to measure 120 teams once, then replay hundreds of searches for free, each tested against shuffled data so luck cannot pass for skill.
Before real money is spent, a rehearsal runs the whole plan against a simulated provider, for $0.

scenes.title: ESP, LEAF, and what comes next

lines.text: A word on names. In the original ESP paper, the part that proposes solutions, the Prescriptor, is itself a learned model.
Here it is not. It is the seven mutations, plus selection.
So in shape this is closer to LEAF, Cognizant's method for evolving neural networks, with agents where LEAF had layers.
There is now a seam for the next step: describe a workload (mostly totals, or mostly linking facts across documents) plus a price cap, and it picks a team for that.
Learning that choice is future work, and the project says so.
You can try it without any account or key. Install it with pip.
make validate runs the linter, the full test suite and an offline search.
make offline breeds and ranks candidates with zero AI calls. make holdout shows the select-and-judge split.
Add a key for Gemini, Claude or GPT, and make smoke sends four questions to a team, end to end.
It also runs as a service. An hourly agent spends what the budget allows, saves after every candidate, and stops. And a web page lets you ask a team a question, and measure teams.
It has limits, and it lists them.
One task domain. So it measures stability across questions, not transfer to new kinds of work.
Only three models measured so far.
And the idea itself is not new. Research like AgentSquare also uses a predictor to search agent designs. What is new is doing it for neuro-san, which had no fitness function at all.
Every number in the README is recomputed from committed data by a test, so the docs cannot quietly drift from the evidence.
Let's recap. neuro-san builds teams of AI agents from a sentence.
This project measures them, on an invented company no model has seen.
It searches for better teams by evolution, with a cheap Predictor deciding which few are worth paying for.
And it proves results on questions it never chose with.
The best team so far: two agents, with the strong model where the reading happens.
The code is open source on GitHub. Thanks for watching.
